dossiers.sanctions.tldr.3: According to the landmark study by Hufbauer, Schott and Elliott, sanctions achieve their goal in about a third of cases (40 out of 115 between 1914 and 1990), especially when the objective is modest [3].
dossiers.sanctions.tldr.4: The United States has a unique weapon: the dollar. In 2014, BNP Paribas pleaded guilty and paid nearly $9 billion for transactions involving Sudan, Iran and Cuba [7].
dossiers.sanctions.sections.0.title: The toolbox
dossiers.sanctions.sections.0.paragraphs: There are several types of sanctions: embargoes (banning the purchase or sale of certain products), asset freezes (blocking money held abroad), travel bans for certain individuals, or exclusion from the international financial system.
They can target an entire country or specific targets: oligarchs, arms companies, banks.

We also distinguish between ==trade== sanctions (on goods), ==financial== sanctions (on money, banks, investments) and ==technology== sanctions (banning the sale of chips, software, machines). Financial sanctions are often the most effective, because almost all world trade goes through a handful of currencies and a handful of banking networks.

Who imposes sanctions? The ==UN Security Council== can impose sanctions binding on every country in the world, but each of its five permanent members (United States, China, Russia, France, United Kingdom) can block a decision with its veto. That is why most sanctions today are decided by ==individual countries or groups of countries==, such as the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom or the G7 [1].
dossiers.sanctions.sections.1.title: A very old weapon
dossiers.sanctions.sections.1.paragraphs: Sanctions are almost as old as trade. Around 432 BCE, Athens barred merchants from the neighbouring city of Megara from its ports and markets. The Greek historian Thucydides lists this ==“Megarian Decree”== among the tensions that led to the Peloponnesian War.

In 1806, Napoleon launched the ==Continental System==: he banned the parts of Europe he controlled from trading with the United Kingdom, in order to ruin its economy. The blockade was widely evaded through smuggling, hurt European ports themselves, and pushed Napoleon to invade Russia in 1812 when Russia refused to enforce it.
These two examples already show the two weaknesses of sanctions: ==they can cause war instead of preventing it==, and ==they only work if everyone enforces them==.
dossiers.sanctions.sections.2.title: 1935: the sanctions that forgot oil
dossiers.sanctions.sections.2.paragraphs: On 3 October 1935, Mussolini's Italy invaded Ethiopia. On 11 October, the ==League of Nations==, the forerunner of the UN, voted economic sanctions against Italy: it was the first time an international organisation had sanctioned one of its own members [4].

But the sanctions left out the essential: ==oil, which the Italian army badly needed, was not on the list== [4]. The United Kingdom and France did not close the Suez Canal either, through which Italian troops passed. And the United States, which was not a member of the League of Nations, kept trading with Italy [4].

In December 1935, it emerged that the British and French ministers, Samuel Hoare and Pierre Laval, had secretly proposed handing part of Ethiopia over to Italy. The scandal finished off the credibility of the effort. Italy conquered Ethiopia and ==the sanctions were lifted in July 1936== [4].

For many historians, this failure showed Hitler that the democracies would not follow through. ==A half-enforced sanction can be worse than no sanction at all==, because it reveals the weakness of those who impose it.
dossiers.sanctions.sections.3.title: 1941: the embargo that led to Pearl Harbor
dossiers.sanctions.sections.3.paragraphs: In July 1941, Japan, at war in China, occupied southern French Indochina. On 25-26 July, the United States ==froze Japanese assets== on its soil; on 1 August, it banned oil exports to aggressor countries [5]. The United Kingdom and the Netherlands, which controlled Indonesia's oil, followed suit.

At the time, Japan imported the vast majority of its oil, most of it from the United States: depending on the source, it lost access to 80 to 90% of its imports [5]. Its leaders calculated that their stocks would not last two years.

They had two options: ==withdraw from Indochina and China to get the sanctions lifted, or seize Southeast Asia's oil by force==, which meant neutralising the American fleet [5]. They chose war: on 7 December 1941 came the attack on Pearl Harbor.

Historians debate exactly how much the embargo weighed in this decision, but the example has become a classic: ==a sanction that threatens a country's survival can push it to strike rather than give in==.
dossiers.sanctions.sections.3.plain.titl: why a sanction can cause a war
dossiers.sanctions.sections.3.plain.step: The United States cuts off Japan's oil to force it to stop expanding [5].
Japan calculates that it has less than two years of stocks left: it must choose quickly.
Giving in means losing face and its conquests; taking Indonesia's oil means war with the United States.
It chooses war: Pearl Harbor, 7 December 1941. The sanction did not make Japan back down; it sped up its decision.
dossiers.sanctions.sections.4.title: The Cold War and apartheid
dossiers.sanctions.sections.4.paragraphs: After 1945, sanctions became a common tool. In ==1962==, the United States imposed a ==total embargo on Cuba==, after the Castro revolution and the nationalisation of American property. More than sixty years later, it is still in place, and so is the Cuban regime: it is the most cited example of a sanction that lasts without achieving its goal.

By contrast, the sanctions against ==apartheid South Africa== are often cited as a partial success. In the 1980s, many countries, companies and universities pulled out of the country or cut their investments; in 1986, the US Congress passed sanctions despite President Reagan's veto. The South African economy suffered, and the regime negotiated the end of apartheid in the early 1990s.

The difference? In South Africa, ==the sanctions came alongside strong internal pressure== (liberation movements, strikes, the Church) and hit an economic elite that had a lot to lose. In Cuba, they instead allowed the regime to blame the United States for the country's difficulties.
dossiers.sanctions.sections.5.title: Iraq in the 1990s and the birth of “targeted” sanctions
dossiers.sanctions.sections.5.paragraphs: After Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, the UN imposed on Iraq some of the harshest sanctions in history: almost all trade was banned. Saddam Hussein's regime stayed in power, but the population suffered badly: shortages of medicine, malnutrition, the collapse of public services. From 1996, an ==“oil-for-food”== programme allowed Iraq to sell oil to buy basic necessities.

The conclusion was shocking: ==broad sanctions mainly hurt civilians, not leaders==. Hence the rise, in the 2000s, of ==“targeted” or “smart” sanctions==: assets are frozen and travel is banned for specific people (leaders, oligarchs, military officers), and specific sectors (arms, oil, banks) are targeted rather than an entire country.
This is the model that dominates today, with lists of thousands of names and companies, regularly updated by the European Union, the United States or the United Kingdom [1].
dossiers.sanctions.sections.6.title: The financial weapon: SWIFT and the dollar
dossiers.sanctions.sections.6.paragraphs: ==SWIFT== is a Belgium-based cooperative that runs the secure messaging system used by more than 11,000 banks around the world for their international transfers [2]. It is not a bank, but without it, a transfer between two countries becomes very complicated.

On ==17 March 2012==, for the first time, SWIFT disconnected banks at the request of the authorities: some thirty Iranian banks targeted by European sanctions over Iran's nuclear programme [6]. Its CEO called it an “extraordinary and unprecedented” step [6].

The United States has an even more powerful weapon: ==the dollar==. Almost all dollar payments pass at some point through American banks, which are subject to American law. A foreign bank that carries out dollar transactions with a country sanctioned by Washington therefore risks prosecution, even if its own country has banned nothing. This is called ==extraterritoriality==, or “secondary sanctions” (see our course on the dollar).

A striking example: in ==2014==, the French bank ==BNP Paribas== pleaded guilty in the United States and agreed to pay ==nearly $8.9 billion== for routing dollar payments linked to Sudan, Iran and Cuba between 2004 and 2012 [7]. At the time, it was the largest penalty ever obtained by the US justice system in an economic sanctions case [7]. For Europe, it was a shock: its companies depend on Washington's decisions.
dossiers.sanctions.sections.7.title: The case of Russia
dossiers.sanctions.sections.7.paragraphs: After February 2022, the European Union, the United States and their allies adopted unprecedented sanctions: a freeze on the Russian central bank's reserves, the exclusion of banks from SWIFT (the messaging system that enables international transfers), an embargo on Russian oil shipped by sea and a cap on its price.
Europe also sharply reduced its purchases of Russian gas, on which it depended heavily, which contributed to the surge in energy prices.

On ==5 December 2022==, two measures came into force together: the European embargo on most imports of Russian oil by ship, and a ==price cap of $60 a barrel== decided by the G7, the EU and Australia [8]. The idea is clever: rather than banning Russian oil for the whole world (which would send prices soaring), other countries are allowed to buy it, provided they pay less than $60; otherwise, Western insurers and shippers are not allowed to handle it [8].

The frozen Russian reserves raise an unprecedented question: what should be done with this money? Confiscating it would be legally risky and could worry other countries that keep their reserves in the West. In June 2024, the G7 found a compromise: a ==$50 billion loan to Ukraine==, repaid using the interest earned on the frozen Russian assets, without touching the capital [9]. Most of these assets are held at Euroclear, in Belgium [9].
dossiers.sanctions.sections.8.title: Do they work?
dossiers.sanctions.sections.8.paragraphs: Yes and no. Russia has lost access to technologies and to part of its revenue. But it has redirected its oil sales to China and India, and uses a “shadow fleet” of old tankers to get around the rules.
This is the limit of sanctions: the more countries enforce them, the more effective they are. And they also have a cost for those who impose them.

The landmark study on the subject, by economists Gary Hufbauer, Jeffrey Schott and Kimberly Elliott, catalogues the sanctions of the 20th century. In its second edition, it finds that sanctions achieved their goal in ==40 out of 115 cases between 1914 and 1990, or about a third== [3]. Modest objectives (freeing a prisoner, winning a concession) succeed far more often than major ones (regime change, ending a war) [3].

This figure is disputed: political scientist Robert Pape argues that only 5 of the 40 successes are genuine, the others being explained mainly by the threat of force [3]. Remember that ==sanctions rarely work on their own==: they work best when they are fast, broad, aimed at a specific objective and backed by diplomacy.
dossiers.sanctions.sections.8.example.te: Studies highlight a few factors: 1) a limited and clear objective; 2) many countries enforcing the sanction (otherwise the target country trades elsewhere); 3) a target country that depends heavily on those imposing sanctions; 4) elites who are personally affected; 5) a way out: what must be done for the sanction to be lifted.
dossiers.sanctions.sections.9.title: Unintended effects
dossiers.sanctions.sections.9.paragraphs: ==The “rally round the flag” effect==: a sanctioned regime can unite its population around it by blaming foreigners for the hardship. ==The black market== often enriches those close to power, who control smuggling.

==De-dollarisation==: by repeatedly using the dollar as a weapon, the United States is pushing some countries (China, Russia, Iran) to develop other payment channels, buy gold and trade in their own currencies. In the long run, financial sanctions could weaken the very tool that makes them possible.

==The costs at home==: European companies that left Russia in 2022 lost billions, and European households paid more for energy. A sanction is never free, which makes coalitions fragile when a crisis drags on.
Finally, ==sanctions are rarely lifted==. Once in place, lifting them looks like a reward or an admission of failure. Many last for decades, like the embargo on Cuba.
dossiers.sanctions.forMe: When you hear about a “new package of sanctions”, ask four questions: what is the objective? Who is enforcing it, and who is not? Who pays the price, including here at home? And what does the target country have to do for the sanctions to be lifted?

dossiers.dollar.hook: Oil is sold in dollars, central banks stockpile dollars, 88% of currency trades involve the dollar… How did the name of a Bohemian silver coin become the planet's currency? From the Spanish piece of eight to the “exorbitant privilege”, from Nixon's gamble in 1971 to central banks' rush for gold.
dossiers.dollar.tldr.0: The dollar is the main reserve currency: nearly 60% of central banks' foreign exchange reserves are in dollars [1]. It is on one side of 88% of all currency transactions worldwide [2].
dossiers.dollar.tldr.1: Its name comes from the “thaler”, a silver coin minted from 1519-1520 in Joachimsthal, Bohemia [3]. Before it was American, the “dollar” referred to the Spanish eight-real coin.
dossiers.dollar.tldr.2: Its dominance dates back to the Bretton Woods agreements (1944). In 1965, de Gaulle called for a return to gold [4]; on 15 August 1971, Nixon suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold [5].
dossiers.dollar.tldr.3: It gives the United States an “exorbitant privilege”: borrowing more cheaply and being able to sanction other countries through its financial system.
dossiers.dollar.tldr.4: Central banks have been buying more than 1,000 tonnes of gold a year since 2022 [6], and in the first half of 2025 the dollar had its worst start to a year since 1973 [7]. But no currency can replace it yet.
dossiers.dollar.sections.0.title: From a Bohemian mine to the piece of eight
dossiers.dollar.sections.0.paragraphs.0: The word ==“dollar”== comes from a small mining town in Bohemia, now in the Czech Republic: Joachimsthal (Jáchymov). In the early 16th century, large silver coins were minted there from local mines, the ==“Joachimsthaler”==, soon shortened to ==“thaler”== [3]. The word spread into neighbouring languages: “daler”, then “dollar” in English around 1600 [3].
dossiers.dollar.sections.0.paragraphs.1: English colonists in America then gave the name “dollar” to another coin, at the time the most widespread in the world: ==the Spanish eight-real coin==, minted with silver from the mines of Mexico and Peru [3]. It was sometimes cut into eight pieces to make change, hence the expression “pieces of eight”.
dossiers.dollar.sections.0.paragraphs.2: When the United States created its currency in 1792, it adopted this familiar name. The irony of history: ==the currency that dominates the world is named after a European coin and began life by imitating a Spanish currency==.
dossiers.dollar.sections.0.paragraphs.3: Before 1914, however, it was not the dollar that reigned but ==the pound sterling==, the currency of the leading commercial and financial power, the United Kingdom. The United States did not even have a central bank until the Federal Reserve was created in 1913.
dossiers.dollar.sections.1.title: 1944: Bretton Woods, the dollar at the centre
dossiers.dollar.sections.1.paragraphs.0: At the end of the Second World War, 44 countries met at Bretton Woods, in the United States. They decided that their currencies would be pegged to the dollar, which itself was convertible into gold.
dossiers.dollar.sections.1.paragraphs.1: Two plans clashed. Britain's ==John Maynard Keynes== proposed a new international currency, the “bancor”, managed by a world bank, so that no country would have an advantage. America's ==Harry Dexter White== wanted to put the dollar at the centre. The United States, which then held most of the world's gold and came out of the war as everyone's creditor, imposed its plan.
dossiers.dollar.sections.1.paragraphs.2: The system worked like this: ==$35 = one ounce of gold==, and the other currencies had a fixed rate against the dollar. Central banks therefore kept their reserves in dollars, which they could in principle exchange for gold with the United States. Bretton Woods also created the IMF and the World Bank.
dossiers.dollar.sections.1.paragraphs.3: For twenty-five years, this system accompanied the strongest growth in the history of Europe and Japan. But it rested on a fragile promise: that the United States would always have enough gold for all the dollars in circulation.
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.title: The “exorbitant privilege” and de Gaulle's anger
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.paragraphs.0: The expression comes from French minister Valéry Giscard d'Estaing in the 1960s, inspired by the economist Jacques Rueff [4]. Since everyone needs dollars, the United States can borrow more cheaply and finance its deficits more easily.
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.paragraphs.1: Another advantage: almost all dollar payments pass, at some point, through American banks. This gives Washington powerful leverage to sanction countries or companies.
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.paragraphs.2: In 1960, Belgian economist Robert Triffin put his finger on a contradiction, the ==“Triffin dilemma”==: for the world to have enough dollars, the United States must issue ever more of them, and therefore spend more abroad than it earns; but the more dollars there are outside the country, the less people believe there will be enough gold to redeem them.
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.paragraphs.3: On ==4 February 1965==, at a press conference, General ==de Gaulle== called for a gradual return to gold as the basis of the international monetary system, because gold belongs to no country [4]. France converted part of its dollars into gold and brought its gold home from New York [4]. The US Treasury replied the same day that the gold standard had “collapsed” in 1931 [4].
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.plain.title: the Triffin dilemma
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.plain.steps.0: World trade grows: countries need more dollars for their reserves and their trade.
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.plain.steps.1: To supply these dollars, the United States must send more of them abroad than it receives: it runs a deficit.
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.plain.steps.2: The dollars held abroad end up exceeding the gold the United States owns.
dossiers.dollar.sections.2.plain.steps.3: Countries start to doubt and demand gold, like France in 1965 [4]: the system cracks.
dossiers.dollar.sections.3.title: 15 August 1971: “our currency, your problem”
dossiers.dollar.sections.3.paragraphs.0: In the 1960s, spending on the Vietnam War and social programmes swelled US deficits. Gold reserves melted away. In August 1971, the United Kingdom in turn asked for a guarantee on its dollars [5].
dossiers.dollar.sections.3.paragraphs.1: On the evening of Sunday ==15 August 1971==, President ==Richard Nixon== announced on television the ==suspension of the dollar's convertibility into gold==, along with a freeze on prices and wages and a surcharge on imports [5]. This was the “Nixon shock”: the Bretton Woods promise was broken unilaterally.
dossiers.dollar.sections.3.paragraphs.2: A few months later, facing furious Europeans, Treasury Secretary ==John Connally== reportedly came out with a now-famous line: ==“The dollar is our currency, but it's your problem”== [5]. It sums up the American attitude: the dollar's swings are decided in Washington, and it is up to the rest of the world to adapt.
dossiers.dollar.sections.3.paragraphs.3: In 1973, the major currencies began to ==float== freely against one another. You might have thought that the dollar, now without gold behind it, would lose its place. The opposite happened: the habit had set in, and ==the dollar remained the reference currency for trade and finance==. That same year, the oil shock and the agreement with Saudi Arabia made the dollar the currency of oil (see our article on the petrodollar).
dossiers.dollar.sections.4.title: Why everyone holds dollars
dossiers.dollar.sections.4.paragraphs.0: A currency dominates when it fulfils three roles on a global scale: ==medium of exchange== (people pay in dollars), ==unit of account== (prices are set in dollars: oil, wheat, copper, aircraft) and ==store of value== (people keep their savings in dollars). The dollar ticks all three boxes.
dossiers.dollar.sections.4.paragraphs.1: The figures show it. At the end of 2024, about ==58% of central banks' declared foreign exchange reserves== were in dollars, compared with about 20% for the euro [1]. And the dollar is ==on one side of 88% of all currency transactions== worldwide, a share that has been stable for ten years [2]: to swap pesos for won, you often go through the dollar.
dossiers.dollar.sections.4.paragraphs.2: Why? The United States offers what no one else offers on the same scale: ==the world's largest government debt market==, highly liquid (billions can be bought and sold in minutes), a freely convertible currency, the rule of law, a powerful military, and habit. ==The more a currency is used, the more useful it becomes==: it is a network effect, as with a language or a social network.
dossiers.dollar.sections.4.paragraphs.3: Some countries even adopt the dollar as their official currency, like Ecuador in 2000 or El Salvador in 2001, after crises that had destroyed confidence in their own currency.
dossiers.dollar.sections.4.example.title: A trade that goes through the dollar
dossiers.dollar.sections.4.example.text: A Chilean company wants to pay a Korean supplier. The direct market between Chilean pesos and Korean won is small and expensive. So it converts its pesos into dollars, then the dollars into won. The dollar serves as a “common language”: that is why it appears in 88% of currency trades [2].
dossiers.dollar.sections.5.title: The flip side of the privilege
dossiers.dollar.sections.5.paragraphs.0: The dollar's global role does not only bring advantages for the United States. Strong demand for dollars ==pushes up the value of the US currency==, which hurts American companies' exports and favours imports: some economists see this as one cause of America's industrial decline.
dossiers.dollar.sections.5.paragraphs.1: For the rest of the world, ==the Fed's decisions become global decisions==. When the Fed raises its rates, the dollar rises, capital leaves emerging countries, and countries with dollar debt see that debt grow heavier. The Latin American debt crisis of 1982, after the Volcker shock, is the classic example (see our article on Reaganomics).
dossiers.dollar.sections.5.paragraphs.2: The strong dollar has sometimes been judged too strong by the United States itself: on ==22 September 1985==, at the Plaza Accord in New York, the major countries agreed to bring the dollar down.
dossiers.dollar.sections.6.title: The dollar as a weapon
dossiers.dollar.sections.6.paragraphs.0: Because almost all dollar transactions pass through American banks, the United States can ==cut a country, a company or a person off from the global financial system==. A foreign bank that works with a country sanctioned by Washington risks being sanctioned itself (see our course on sanctions).
dossiers.dollar.sections.6.paragraphs.1: This weapon has been used against Iran, North Korea, Venezuela and, on an unprecedented scale, against Russia in 2022: the Russian central bank's reserves held in the West were frozen. The message was heard around the world: ==dollar reserves can become unusable overnight== if you fall out with Washington.
dossiers.dollar.sections.6.paragraphs.2: Therein lies the paradox: ==the more the United States uses the dollar as a weapon, the more it encourages others to look for alternatives==.
dossiers.dollar.sections.7.title: The end of King Dollar?
dossiers.dollar.sections.7.paragraphs.0: China, Russia and other BRICS countries are trying to trade more in their own currencies, partly to escape US sanctions. Some central banks are also buying a lot of gold.
dossiers.dollar.sections.7.paragraphs.1: These gold purchases are spectacular: central banks bought ==more than 1,000 tonnes a year in 2022, 2023 and 2024==, something never seen before, compared with an average of about 470 tonnes a year between 2010 and 2021 [6]. Gold has an advantage the dollar lacks: it belongs to no country and cannot be frozen if it is stored at home.
dossiers.dollar.sections.7.paragraphs.2: In the first half of 2025, ==the dollar lost about 10.8% against the major currencies, its worst start to a year since 1973== [7], against a backdrop of tariffs, worries about US debt and political pressure on the Fed [7]. Some see this as the start of a decline.
dossiers.dollar.sections.7.paragraphs.3: But replacing the dollar is hard: it takes a freely convertible currency, huge financial markets and investor confidence. For now, no alternative has all of this, with the euro still far behind. The ==Chinese yuan== is gaining ground (it was the 5th most traded currency in 2022, with 7% of transactions [2]), but China controls capital flows, which holds back its use as a reserve currency.
dossiers.dollar.sections.8.title: What about the euro?
dossiers.dollar.sections.8.paragraphs.0: Launched in 1999, the euro has become the ==world's second currency==: about 20% of foreign exchange reserves [1] and 31% of currency transactions in 2022 [2]. It is the currency of more than 340 million Europeans and the pivot of trade in much of Africa and Eastern Europe.
dossiers.dollar.sections.8.paragraphs.1: But it lacks some of the dollar's strengths: ==no large single government debt market== (each country issues its own bonds, of varying quality), no common army, and governance shared among more than twenty countries, which is slower. The creation of common European debt during Covid (the 2020 recovery plan) was seen as a step in that direction.
dossiers.dollar.sections.8.paragraphs.2: Remember the lesson of history: the pound sterling took decades to give way to the dollar, even after the United States had overtaken Britain economically. ==Dominant currencies decline slowly==, and the dollar is still well ahead.
dossiers.dollar.forMe: The price of filling up your tank, your phone or your plane ticket depends partly on the dollar: when it rises against the euro, everything paid for in dollars costs more in Europe. And when the Fed sets its rates in Washington, your purchasing power moves too.

dossiers.dollar.quiz.7.q: Why have central banks been buying so much gold since 2022?
dossiers.dollar.quiz.7.options.1: To diversify their reserves, because gold belongs to no country and cannot be frozen if it is stored at home
dossiers.dollar.quiz.7.explain: More than 1,000 tonnes a year in 2022, 2023 and 2024, after Russia's reserves were frozen.

resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.lines.0.label: Revenue
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.lines.1.label: Adjusted earnings per share
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.guidance.text: Nvidia had set itself a target of $108 billion in revenue for this quarter, plus or minus 2%, with a targeted gross margin of 74% [1].
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.summary: Nvidia's first earnings report without Jensen Huang: the founder left the top job on 12 November, and chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim leader [3][4].
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.points.0: Analysts expect a little more than the company's target: about $108.8 billion in revenue according to MarketBeat, and adjusted earnings per share of about $2.49 according to Zacks (13 estimates, ranging from $2.34 to $2.70) [1][2].
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.points.1: Nvidia beat the Zacks consensus in each of its last four quarters [2]: a result merely “within the range” could therefore disappoint.
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.points.2: The most closely watched figure will be the target for the following quarter, which shows whether demand for artificial intelligence chips is still accelerating [1].
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.points.3: According to LSEG, cited by Boursorama, the consensus is for about $109 billion in revenue [5].
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.points.4: Banks are divided: Wedbush expects revenue above forecasts and a strong outlook for the following quarter [6], RBC speaks of “robust” demand [7], while Bernstein has downgraded its rating to “neutral” [8].
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.points.5: The stock has lost more than 30% since its all-time high, mainly on fears of a slowdown in AI data centres [8].
resultats.nvidia-t3-2027.points.6: The board of directors announced the departure of Jensen Huang, CEO and board member, with immediate effect, and named Harvey C. Jones as first chairman of the board [3]. The share price fell as much as 13% after the announcement before partly recovering [4].
resultats.home-depot-t3-2026.summary: The American home improvement giant gives news of the housing market: when few homes are selling, big renovation projects get put off [2].
resultats.home-depot-t3-2026.points.0: Analysts expect earnings per share of $3.84 (+2.7% year on year) on revenue of $42.8 billion (+3.4%) [1]. Zacks is slightly more cautious, at $3.81 [2].
resultats.home-depot-t3-2026.points.1: As long as home sales do not pick up, demand should stay focused on small jobs, which limits big renovation purchases [2].
resultats.home-depot-t3-2026.points.2: Results released before Wall Street opens, conference call at 9 a.m. New York time [3].
resultats.target-t3-2026.summary: Target reports the day before Walmart: together, they show how American household spending is holding up ahead of the holidays [1].
resultats.target-t3-2026.points.0: Results expected before Wall Street opens, on Wednesday 18 November [1][2].
resultats.target-t3-2026.points.1: What to watch: comparable-store sales and what the retailer says about the holiday season, which weighs heavily in its year [1].
resultats.walmart-t3-2027.lines.0.label: Revenue
resultats.walmart-t3-2027.lines.1.label: Adjusted earnings per share
resultats.walmart-t3-2027.guidance.text: For the full fiscal year, Walmart is targeting earnings per share of $2.80 to $2.87 and revenue growth of 4 to 5% [2].
resultats.walmart-t3-2027.summary: The world's largest retailer serves as a thermometer of American consumer spending: when households tighten their belts, they come to Walmart [2].
resultats.walmart-t3-2027.points.0: Analysts expect earnings per share of 63 cents (+1.6% year on year) on revenue of $187.2 billion (+5.3%) [1].
resultats.walmart-t3-2027.points.1: A Bank of America analyst expects Walmart to raise its annual target towards the top of its range [2].
resultats.walmart-t3-2027.points.2: Date taken from stock market calendars: Walmart usually reports on a Thursday, before the opening bell [1].
resultats.amd-t3-2026.lines.0.label: Revenue
resultats.amd-t3-2026.lines.1.label: Adjusted earnings per share
resultats.amd-t3-2026.lines.2.label: Q4 revenue target
resultats.amd-t3-2026.guidance.text: AMD is targeting about $17 billion in revenue in the fourth quarter, plus or minus 3%, above the $16.3 billion expected. The only cloud: a targeted gross margin of about 55%, slightly below the 55.5% hoped for [3].
resultats.amd-t3-2026.summary: Record revenue, driven by data centres, and a year-end target well above expectations [1][3].
resultats.amd-t3-2026.points.0: Revenue of $13.38 billion, up about 45% year on year, compared with $13.11 billion expected according to S&P data cited by StockStory [1].
resultats.amd-t3-2026.points.1: Data centres, where AMD sells its artificial intelligence chips, reached a record $8.5 billion, almost double a year earlier (+97%) [1].
resultats.amd-t3-2026.points.2: Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.09, compared with $1.95 expected [2]. Under US accounting standards (GAAP), they were $1.46, for net income of $2.4 billion and a gross margin of 54% [4][5].
resultats.amd-t3-2026.points.3: What pleased investors most: the target for the following quarter. A jump from $13.4 billion to about $17 billion in one quarter shows that orders for AI chips are coming in [3].
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.lines.0.label: Adjusted net earnings
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.lines.1.label: Uranium production for the quarter
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.guidance.text: Cameco now only expects to produce 19.5 to 20.5 million pounds of uranium this year, compared with 19.5 to 21.5 million before: the top of the range is gone [2].
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.move.text: on the Toronto Stock Exchange on results day, at C$107.60 [3]
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.summary: The Canadian uranium giant disappoints: a mine shut down for longer than planned caused production to drop 20% [2].
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.points.0: Results below analysts' expectations [4]. Excluding one-off items, Cameco posted a small loss of C$2 million, compared with a profit of C$32 million a year earlier; reported net earnings were C$43 million, or C$0.10 per share [1][2].
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.points.1: The main cause: an extended maintenance shutdown at Key Lake, in Saskatchewan, which brought the quarter's production down to 3.5 million pounds of uranium, 20% less than a year earlier [2].
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.points.2: Lower sales, higher unit costs and smaller gains from its stake in Westinghouse also weighed, partly offset by higher selling prices [2][5]. Revenue for the quarter was C$619 million [5].
resultats.cameco-t3-2026.points.3: Cameco is maintaining an annual dividend of C$0.24 per share, paid on 15 December [2].
resultats.cn-t3-2026.lines.0.label: Revenue
resultats.cn-t3-2026.lines.1.label: Adjusted earnings per share
resultats.cn-t3-2026.guidance.text: CN is keeping its target of adjusted earnings per share growth “in the mid-to-high single digits” this year, and says it is heading towards the top of that range [1].
resultats.cn-t3-2026.summary: Canada's largest rail network is carrying more and earning more: revenue up 15%, above expectations [1][2].
resultats.cn-t3-2026.points.0: Revenue of C$4,771 million, up C$606 million (+15%) year on year [1], compared with about C$4.63 billion expected according to Investing.com [2] and C$4.66 billion according to FactSet [3].
resultats.cn-t3-2026.points.1: Adjusted earnings per share of C$2.16, up 18% [1], compared with C$2.09 expected according to FactSet [3]. Net income of C$1,209 million, compared with C$1,139 million a year earlier [3].
resultats.cn-t3-2026.points.2: Volumes carried, measured in gross ton-miles, rose by about 4%, and CN bought back about 3.9 million of its shares for C$676 million during the quarter [3].
resultats.cn-t3-2026.points.3: The adjusted operating ratio, the share of revenue eaten up by costs, improved to 61.0% (0.4 points better) [1].
resultats.cn-t3-2026.points.4: Good news for the coming months: CN now expects 2026-2027 grain harvests above their five-year average, and therefore more grain to carry [1].
resultats.totalenergies-t3-2026.summary: Record profit for the French group, driven by soaring oil and gas prices and refining margins [1][5].
resultats.totalenergies-t3-2026.points.0: Adjusted net income of $9.1 billion, compared with $8.9 billion expected by analysts polled by the group, and more than double a year earlier [2].
resultats.totalenergies-t3-2026.points.1: It beats every consensus: $8.9 billion expected by analysts polled by the group [2], $8.73 billion according to Visible Alpha [4], and $8.3 billion on average for the 12 analysts in the LSEG consensus [3].
resultats.totalenergies-t3-2026.points.2: It is also up sharply from the second quarter, when it stood at $6.0 billion [2].
resultats.totalenergies-t3-2026.points.3: Reported net income reached $8.3 billion, compared with $3.7 billion in the third quarter of 2025 [1].
resultats.totalenergies-t3-2026.points.4: Refining and liquefied natural gas drove the quarter, with a refining margin of $33.2 per tonne [1]. Refining generated $3.60 billion, more than double a year earlier, and LNG earnings were multiplied by 2.3, to $1.9 billion [4].
resultats.totalenergies-t3-2026.points.5: The debt ratio fell to 9.1%, 4 points better than in the second quarter [4].
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.lines.0.label: Revenue
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.lines.1.label: Earnings per share
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.guidance.text: Alphabet is keeping its 2026 capital spending forecast unchanged, despite the drop in its cash flow [3].
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.summary: Google narrowly misses on revenue and clearly misses on profit: cloud is booming, but search and YouTube disappoint [1][2].
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.points.0: Revenue of about $127.6 billion, up 25%, below expectations: $127.9 billion according to Newsquawk [2], $128.2 billion according to the LSEG consensus [5].
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.points.1: Earnings of $2.12 per share, down about 26% year on year, compared with $3.02 expected according to FactSet; the gap comes largely from a loss of about $8.7 billion on investments [1][5]. Even excluding one-off items, adjusted earnings ($2.67) remain below consensus [5].
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.points.2: Google Cloud more than doubled year on year and beat expectations, but advertising ($82 billion) fell short: AI mode in search is slowing search-related ads [4][5].
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.points.3: Spending on AI data centres is weighing: $51.4 billion in capital expenditure for the quarter, and negative free cash flow of about $9.1 billion [3][5].
resultats.alphabet-t3-2026.points.4: The next morning, the stock was still down about 10% before Wall Street opened [6].
